extracted.intended_audience: state environmental agencies, regulated electric utility owners/operators, legal advisers, and stakeholders participating in EPA CAA section 111 rulemakings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how EPA (and states implementing EPA emission guidelines) must identify the Best System of Emission Reduction (BSER) and set/translate that BSER into achievable standards of performance for new and existing stationary source categories under CAA section 111.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approach to the Source Category and Subcategorizing
rubrics_metrics.description: CAA section 111 requires EPA to list stationary source categories and gives EPA discretion to "distinguish among classes, types, and sizes within categories" (i.e., subcategorize) when establishing standards for new sources; EPA has likewise interpreted section 111(d) to permit subcategorization for existing sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA is entitled to a high degree of deference in subcategorization because it entails scientific judgment. Subcategorization may be based on size, type, fuel combusted, equipment, manufacturing processes, levels of utilization, activity level, geographic location, costs of control, physical limitations, or similar factors. EPA's historic regulations (40 FR 53340) and multiple rulemakings demonstrate a long practice of subcategorizing; examples include heat-input capacity, fuel type, base-load vs non-base-load turbines, active vs closed landfills, and geographic subdivisions for SO2 rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: System of Emission Reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify one or more "system[s] of emission reduction" that have been adequately demonstrated for the source category and determine which of these is the "best" for purposes of setting standards of performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although not statutorily defined, historically EPA has looked to measures that improve the pollution performance of individual sources (a technology-based approach) such as efficiency improvements, fuel-switching, and add-on controls; the statute also contemplates off-site activities (e.g., precombustion cleaning/treatment of fuels) as a system. Systems should be those that reduce an individual source's overall contribution to pollution. The Supreme Court in West Virginia recognized EPA's historical approach but applied the major questions doctrine to a generation-shifting BSER.

rubrics_metrics.name: “Adequately Demonstrated”
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of emission reduction must be one that the Administrator determines has been "adequately demonstrated" before it can serve as the basis for an "achievable" emission standard under CAA section 111(a)(1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate demonstration requires sufficient evidence (e.g., demonstration projects, pilot tests, commercial-scale operation) to support a reasoned extrapolation that affected sources can adopt the system. The statute and caselaw permit an adequately demonstrated system even if it is not in widespread commercial use at the time of promulgation — i.e., EPA may rely on demonstration projects and extrapolation rather than widespread industry deployment. However, EPA may not base the determination on mere speculation or conjecture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Achievability of the Emission Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard of performance must "reflect the degree of emission limitation achievable through the application of the BSER," meaning the standard must be achievable through application of the identified system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Achievability requires a record-based finding that affected sources can adopt the specified system to attain the degree of emission limitation. Case law allows EPA to set standards more stringent than historically achieved where specific technological improvements support that projection (e.g., extrapolations from pilot/commercial tests). An achievable standard is within the realm of the adequately demonstrated system's efficiency and need not necessarily have been routinely achieved industry-wide before adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory factors to evaluate in selecting the BSER
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must take into account, when determining the BSER and the degree of emission limitation, the cost of achieving the reduction and any non-air quality health and environmental impacts and energy requirements; courts have also identified the amount of air pollution reduced and the role of technological innovation as considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EPA may weigh these factors against each other and has discretion in that weighing. The Agency's approach should evaluate candidate systems on amount of emission reductions, costs, non-air health/environmental impacts, and energy requirements, and then select the "best" system consistent with precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authority to adopt technology‑forcing standards (systems not in widespread use)
rubrics_metrics.description: CAA section 111(a)(1) authorizes EPA to establish standards that encourage broader adoption of more effective systems of emission reduction even if those systems are not yet in widespread commercial use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative history and caselaw support that "adequately demonstrated" does not require widespread commercial deployment; Congress intended CAA section 111 to permit technology‑forcing standards so long as the technology is demonstrated (e.g., via examples, experiments, demonstration plants) and EPA has adequate evidence to extrapolate practical deployment and effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of extrapolation and other qualitative methods when direct data are limited
rubrics_metrics.description: When direct data are unavailable, EPA may reasonably extrapolate from test sources, pilot projects, or related industries to conclude that a system is adequately demonstrated and that a standard is achievable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (e.g., Essex Chem./Ruckelshaus, Lignite Energy Council) permits extrapolation but cautions that EPA may not rely on mere speculation or conjecture; the Agency may compensate for limited quantitative data through reasonable qualitative extrapolation and other evidence showing feasibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance timeframe / deployment feasibility
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA must demonstrate that the industry can deploy the identified BSER at scale within the compliance timeframe before basing standards on that system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing an adequately demonstrated BSER requires not only technical demonstration but also a showing that sources in the category can adopt the system within the period allowed for compliance; this consideration can affect whether EPA sets the system as BSER or tailors compliance times and subcategories.

rubrics_metrics.name: State flexibility in implementing standards of performance
rubrics_metrics.description: After EPA determines the BSER and the degree of emission limitation, states are responsible under section 111(d) for establishing standards of performance for affected existing sources that reflect the degree of emission limitation EPA determined; states retain certain flexibilities in assigning standards and choosing compliance mechanisms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States can tailor how to ensure their standards collectively represent the equivalent of EPA's performance rates (e.g., by establishing standards individually, in the aggregate, or combined with other measures). States may include trading, averaging, or other programmatic compliance mechanisms in their plans, subject to EPA guidance and statutory limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall analytical approach to determining BSER and emission limits
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA's overall approach is to identify systems of emission reduction that have been adequately demonstrated for the category, evaluate those systems on emission reductions, costs, non-air impacts, and energy requirements, determine which is the "best" system, and then set an achievable emission limit based on application of that BSER.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For each subcategory, EPA should follow this stepwise approach and document that identified costs are reasonable and the selected BSER is rational in light of statutory factors and precedent. The process involves (1) system identification, (2) adequacy-of-demonstration evaluation, (3) balancing statutory factors to select the best system, and (4) translating the BSER into achievable standards of performance (including considering subcategories and compliance timing).
